idiom_name: Stream.iterate(T seed, Predicate<? super T> hasNext, UnaryOperator<T> next)
implementation_notes: Java 9's three-argument Stream.iterate is the standard-library unfold for sequences: the seed is the initial state, hasNext is the stop condition and next produces the following state, while the stream stays lazy so the terminal operation decides how much is generated. Use it for linear structures; tree-shaped results are still built recursively or with an explicit Deque worklist and a Stream.Builder, because a stream can only unfold one element per state.
code_sketch:
Stream.iterate(seed, s -> s > 1, s -> s / 2)   // seed, hasNext, next
      .map(Node::new)                          // one layer per state
      .forEach(System.out::println);           // terminal op drives the unfold
pitfalls: Nothing is generated until a terminal operation runs, and an unterminated unfold never returns from toList()/collect - the predicate, not the pipeline, is the guard.
The two-argument iterate(seed, next) is endless by contract: forgetting limit() is an unbounded generation bug that only appears at the terminal operation.
Recursive tree unfolds overflow the stack; use an explicit Deque worklist and Stream.Builder instead.

variants.name: Hand-written Spliterator over the state (Java 8 floor)
variants.idiom_name: Spliterator.OfRef whose tryAdvance applies the step function
variants.implementation_notes: Before the three-argument iterate, the same coalgebra was hand-written: a Spliterator holds the current state and tryAdvance emits one layer while advancing it, with ORDERED | IMMUTABLE characteristics and an unbounded estimate. This remains the way to unfold into a Stream when the state machine does not fit a single UnaryOperator (multi-field state, checked exceptions, several emitted layers per step) or when the Java 8 floor must hold.
pitfalls: AbstractSpliterator reports Long.MAX_VALUE as its estimate size, so batch traversal (forEachRemaining) iterates the whole unfold; bound it explicitly.
Spliterators and their streams are single-use: a second traversal throws IllegalStateException while a reused spliterator silently continues from its mutated state.
